This bill would let the Governor-General declare a national emergency on the Prime Minister's recommendation.
It would create a single list of existing federal emergency powers so decision-makers can see all options, and let ministers cut red tape during a declared emergency.
The Prime Minister could also order Commonwealth agencies to share details on stockpiles, assets and response plans.
Establishes a legal process for the Governor-General to declare a national emergency.
Compiles existing Commonwealth emergency powers into one list for easier access by decision-makers.
Lets ministers suspend or change regulatory requirements in their own legislation if it helps the public during or after a national emergency.
Allows the Prime Minister to require Commonwealth entities to provide information on stockpiles, assets and response options.
The Governor-General, the Prime Minister, Commonwealth ministers and Commonwealth entities are affected.

The majority voted against adding [additional words](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-12-10.58.1) (see below) to the usual [second reading](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/) motion, which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" - parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill. The National Emergency Declaration Bill was introduced to establish a legislative framework for declaring national emergencies, implementing recommendation 5.1 of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements. It allows the Governor-General to declare a national emergency on the Prime Minister’s advice, with a maximum duration of three months (extendable), and creates powers to waive red tape and compel Commonwealth entities to report information during declared emergencies.

The National Emergency Declaration (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2020 amends Commonwealth legislation to streamline emergency powers, enabling ministers and officials to act quickly during a declared national emergency. It implements recommendation 5.1 of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements by removing redundant emergency tests and creating simplified alternative tests for exercising powers.

The National Emergency Declaration Bill 2020 establishes a legislative framework for the Governor-General to declare a national emergency on the Prime Minister's advice, using an all-hazards approach to streamline emergency powers and cut red tape, including amendments to the Sydney Airport Curfew Act and new obligations on telecommunication providers. The speaker criticised the Victorian government's 18-month extension of emergency powers during COVID-19 as failing to balance swift response with accountability.

The speaker supported the National Emergency Declaration Bill 2020, arguing the Commonwealth's response to the Black Summer bushfires was inadequate and that the bill streamlines disaster response, but noted concerns that it was drafted without consulting states and that many royal commission recommendations—such as a sovereign aerial firefighting fleet and a single emergency app—remain unimplemented.

The speaker argued in support of the National Emergency Declaration Bill 2020 and its consequential amendments, which implement recommendation 5.1 of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements. The bills allow the federal government to declare a national emergency for nationally significant harm from any hazard, with safeguards including a three-month limit, state/territory request requirement, ministerial reporting to parliament, and a five-year review.

The National Emergency Declaration Bill 2020 and its companion bill create a legislative framework for the Governor-General to declare a national emergency on the Prime Minister's advice, implementing recommendation 5.1 of the Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements. The bill gives the Prime Minister power to request a declaration unilaterally if a state is incapacitated, allows suspension of procedural requirements for emergency support, and introduces mandatory reviews within five years and after each declaration.
